title: Things to do in Kamakura: 5 temples and shrines to visit
description: Visit five Kamakura places: the Great Buddha, Hasedera, Tsurugaoka Hachimangu, Hokokuji and Zeniarai, with Tokyo trains, admission advice and a practical route.
intro: For a first visit to Kamakura, consider five places with distinct experiences: Kotokuin’s Great Buddha, Hasedera’s gardens and Kannon statue, Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine, the bamboo temple Hokokuji and Zeniarai Benzaiten’s ritual spring. Kotokuin and Hasedera make a close pair in Hase, while Hokokuji and Zeniarai require journeys in different directions. A day trip from Tokyo does not require fitting all five into one busy circuit.

Kamakura is in Kanagawa Prefecture, with rail connections from Tokyo and Yokohama. You can explore Buddhist art, shrines and gardens without changing hotels, but it helps to arrive with priorities. This guide explains what to look for, how Kamakura and Hase stations organize the journey, which admissions are separate and where to shorten your plans. Operator travel times are estimates rather than guarantees; ceremonies, weather and access arrangements can change what works on the day.

quickFacts.label: Location
quickFacts.value: Kamakura, Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, reached by train from Tokyo or Yokohama.

quickFacts.label: From Tokyo
quickFacts.value: The tourist association gives about an hour from Tokyo Station on the JR Yokosuka Line; check services for your date.

quickFacts.label: Close pair
quickFacts.value: Kotokuin and Hasedera are in Hase; Kotokuin estimates roughly five minutes on foot between them.

quickFacts.label: Planning
quickFacts.value: Use Hase for the Great Buddha and Hasedera, and Kamakura Station for the central shrine and the two other journeys.

quickFacts.label: New Year warning
quickFacts.value: Hokokuji lists closure from December 29 to January 3; this selection is not a holiday events programme.

sections.heading: 1. Kotokuin’s Great Buddha: a sculpture beneath the open sky
paragraphs: The Great Buddha of Kamakura is the image of Amida Buddha at Kotokuin. The temple identifies two features that explain its appeal: the large copper sculpture and its open-air setting. Start by looking from the space in front before moving closer to individual details. The relationship between the figure, courtyard and sky lets you appreciate its scale without entering the statue.

Kotokuin is at 4-2-28 Hase. From Kamakura Station, take Enoden towards Fujisawa and get off at Hase, the third stop. The temple estimates a seven-minute walk from the station; that does not include waiting, crowds or time to find your bearings. The simplest pairing in this guide is Hasedera, which Kotokuin places about five minutes away on foot. Save both locations before leaving Hase Station rather than improvising separate journeys back to Kamakura.

Published adult general admission is 300 yen, with an extra 50 yen to enter the Buddha’s interior. The temple says ordinary visits do not require reservations. Going inside is an additional choice with its own admission hours, rather than a requirement for appreciating the sculpture. Check the day’s visitor information and distinguish the final admission time from the closing time. If a queue would disrupt the rest of your plans, the outdoor visit still has its own purpose.

The temple has no car parking. Kotokuin advises that some areas can be difficult for wheelchair users without help and lists an accessible toilet, so ask about the appropriate route if that affects your group. Personal photography is subject to visitor rules; commercial photography requires advance temple permission. Keep circulation routes clear and allow worshippers space rather than turning the courtyard into an extended photo session.

sections.heading: 2. Hasedera: Kannon, gardens and a view towards the sea
paragraphs: Hasedera offers more than a single hall. Its principal image is an eleven-headed Kannon measuring 9.18 metres, according to the temple. The account of two statues carved from one sacred tree is presented as a religious legend and should be understood in that context. This is Kamakura’s Hasedera in Hase, rather than the temple with the same name in Nara. Keep that distinction in mind when checking directions, visitor information and photographs.

Use the temple map to choose a route between the levels. The lower garden, shown in our photograph, rewards attention to ponds and planting; stairs lead to other areas, including Jizo-do Hall. The upper observation platform looks across the town and towards the ocean. If stairs present a difficulty, ask which parts suit your group instead of assuming that every area is step-free. The visit can be organized around the features you can actually reach.

The garden changes with the seasons. Hasedera associates June with its hydrangea path, but a flower calendar cannot guarantee a particular display or identical admission arrangements each year. If hydrangeas are the reason for your journey, check the current flower update and any special instructions before choosing a date. At other times, the Kannon, gardens and viewpoint still provide a varied visit; you do not need to build the whole excursion around a seasonal photograph.

The English and Japanese pages consulted agree on adult general admission of 400 yen. The Kannon Museum has a separate admission. The Japanese access page gives around five minutes on foot from Hase Station. From July to March, the listed closing time is 17:00, with last entry at 16:30; from April to June, both are half an hour later. Check current notices and individual facilities rather than arriving just before the final admission.

sections.heading: 3. Tsurugaoka Hachimangu: Kamakura’s warrior connections
paragraphs: Tsurugaoka Hachimangu brings a change from Hase’s Buddhist art to a shrine connected with Kamakura’s warrior history. The tourist association explains that Minamoto no Yoritomo moved the shrine to its present location and that other warriors followed his devotion to Hachiman. That relationship helps explain the site without treating it as another version of the temples above. Pay attention to the arrangement of the grounds and their religious use as well as the architecture.

The address is 2-1-31 Yukinoshita. The tourist association estimates a ten-minute walk from Kamakura Station’s east exit, making it a useful central visit before or after your Enoden journey. Our photograph shows the Maiden pavilion, with the stairs and principal sanctuary behind it. These are parts of one complex, rather than entrances to interchangeable attractions. Take time to look from the lower level and decide how to continue according to your interests and mobility.

Cultural facilities in the grounds have separate arrangements. The tourist association lists museums and halls with their own opening times and fees, so a shrine visit should not be taken to include every exhibition. If a particular museum interests you, check that service specifically. The priority here is the religious complex; adding an exhibition means reconsidering the time available for other places, rather than counting only the walk from the station.

This is also a sensible point to pause and reassess the day. If you arrived late, keep Hachimangu and the Hase pair, leaving one of the longer journeys for another visit. During ceremonies and celebrations, follow local instructions and make room for worshippers.

sections.heading: 4. Hokokuji: a bamboo garden and a quieter pace
paragraphs: Hokokuji, also written Houkokuji on its website, is a Zen temple within the Kenchoji order of the Rinzai school. Its garden of Moso bamboo creates a different setting from Kotokuin’s large courtyard. Look at the temple as a whole: the photograph in this guide records the main hall, while the bamboo garden is a separate part of the visit. Slow down, remain quiet and observe without leaving the permitted paths or touching the plants.

The temple is at 2-7-4 Jomyoji. Its operator describes taking a Keikyu bus from Kamakura to Jomyoji, spelt Joumyoji on the English page, followed by about three minutes on foot. The tourist association places the bus departure at Kamakura Station’s east exit. Check the service destination and stop before boarding: not every bus from the station serves this journey. The association gives approximately 35 minutes on foot from Kamakura Station as an alternative.

Published general admission is 400 yen. Matcha with a dry sweet costs an additional 600 yen; tea is an option rather than something included in garden admission. The tourist association warns that reception for tea may be temporarily suspended during busy periods. Ask about availability when you arrive instead of arranging the whole day around an assumed seat. Allow yourself to enjoy the garden even if the tea service does not work with your visit.

Hokokuji lists ordinary opening hours of 09:00–16:00 and a final tea order at 15:30, with closure from December 29 to January 3. The operator also warns of closure in bad weather. Do not leave this as a final stop without checking those conditions. Tripods and other camera supports are prohibited, as are crossing fences and touching plants. If weather deteriorates, reconsider the journey before heading out towards Jomyoji.

sections.heading: 5. Zeniarai Benzaiten: a spring and a money-washing tradition
paragraphs: Zeniarai Benzaiten Ugafuku Jinja introduces a specific custom: washing money at a spring, traditionally associated with prosperity. The tourist association connects the site’s origin with a dream of Yoritomo and also mentions Hojo Tokiyori in the tradition. These are religious narratives and beliefs, rather than a financial promise. The visit offers a way to understand the custom and its setting, whether you choose to participate or simply watch respectfully.

The shrine is at 2-25-16 Sasuke. The official visitor reference is approximately 25 minutes on foot from Kamakura Station’s west exit, unlike the east exit used for Hachimangu and the Hokokuji bus. The photograph shows the entrance with torii gates and a tunnel, rather than the spring inside. Save the complete address and use the signed urban approach; including the shrine in this selection does not require connecting it by a mountain hiking trail.

The tourist listing gives final entrance at 16:00, although the site hours extend to 16:30. That distinction matters: arriving at 16:15 does not mean you can enter. The fee field says donation without establishing a fixed price for every ritual action. If you want to participate, ask about the steps and offerings locally. Do not assume any container is suitable or photograph people closely while they are carrying out the practice.

This journey works best when you have time to walk and return without rushing. On a single day, compare its appeal with Hokokuji’s garden and choose according to your priorities. Both offer worthwhile experiences, but moving between them requires reorganizing your travel through Kamakura. Leaving one for another occasion gives you more time at the place you choose, as well as room for a meal and the journey back.

sections.heading: Getting from Tokyo and grouping your journeys
paragraphs: From Tokyo Station, the tourist association describes the JR Yokosuka Line to Kamakura, taking around an hour. It also identifies that line from Yokohama. Check the train, destination and any service disruption before leaving; the estimate does not include travel from your hotel or navigating a large station. The association recommends public transport because roads around visitor sights experience heavy traffic on weekdays as well as weekends.

For Hase, change to Enoden in Kamakura. The official station sequence confirms the connection. Group Kotokuin and Hasedera on foot, then return to Kamakura for the centre. Hachimangu uses the east exit; Zeniarai is approached from the west. Hokokuji requires its own journey towards Jomyoji. Avoid buying a pass automatically: compare the trips you will actually take and check which operators it covers. An Enoden ticket should not be assumed to cover JR or every bus.

sections.heading: Admission, weather and decisions before setting out
paragraphs: As a reference from the pages consulted, Kotokuin, Hasedera and Hokokuji’s general admission total 1,100 yen per adult; the Buddha’s interior and tea are extra. This is not the cost of the whole excursion: transport, food, other facilities and possible offerings remain separate. Confirm prices and payment arrangements for your visit date.

Choose the season according to your interests without expecting guaranteed flowers or clear weather. For Hasedera, check the seasonal calendar and current flower update; for Hokokuji, check the weather and published closures. Wear suitable walking shoes, protect your belongings if rain is forecast and prioritize earlier final admissions. If anyone needs a route without stairs, ask the individual sites and transport operators in advance: a short distance between two points does not establish accessibility.

sections.heading: Photography and respect at places of worship
paragraphs: Kamakura’s visitor guidelines ask for quiet at temples and shrines, respect for photography rules and consideration for residents and pedestrians. Step out of circulation routes when checking your map and carry your rubbish until you can dispose of it properly. Keep to designated paths; this guide does not propose shortcuts across private property or through mountain trails.

Before photographing an interior, ceremony or ritual detail, look for the site’s instructions. Permission for personal pictures does not authorize commercial work or override restrictions on tripods and the privacy of worshippers. The five documentary photographs here help identify the places; they do not guarantee how each site will look on a future travel date.

itinerary: A day trip with three priorities: arrive in Kamakura with time to spare, take Enoden to Hase and visit Kotokuin and Hasedera. Leave time for lunch without putting the next final admission at risk, return by train to Kamakura and walk from the east exit to Tsurugaoka Hachimangu. You can reverse the order to suit the day’s conditions, while keeping temple admission deadlines in mind.

To add a fourth place, choose Zeniarai or Hokokuji and reorganize the day from the outset rather than adding it just before closing. To visit all five with more breathing room, split them: one day for Hase and Hachimangu, another for Zeniarai’s western approach and the journey to Hokokuji, with a break in Kamakura between them. These are planning suggestions, rather than a tour with guaranteed connections.

faq.question: Can you visit Kamakura on a day trip from Tokyo?
faq.answer: Yes. The tourist association gives around an hour from Tokyo Station on the JR Yokosuka Line. Kotokuin, Hasedera and Tsurugaoka Hachimangu make a reasonable core for a first excursion. Check services and notices; visiting all five places requires more time and decisions about travel.

faq.question: Are the Great Buddha and Hasedera close together?
faq.answer: Yes. Kotokuin estimates about five minutes on foot between the two Hase sites. You can reach the neighbourhood on Enoden from Kamakura. Walking estimates help with orientation but do not include waiting, breaks or the time spent visiting each place.

faq.question: Should you choose Hokokuji or Zeniarai when time is short?
faq.answer: Choose Hokokuji for its Zen temple and bamboo garden, or Zeniarai for its spring and money-washing tradition. The former requires a journey towards Jomyoji; the latter is approached from Kamakura Station’s west exit. Decide according to your interests and remaining admission time instead of combining them late in the day.

faq.question: Is matcha included in admission to Hokokuji?
faq.answer: No. The operator lists 400 yen for general admission and a separate 600 yen for matcha with a dry sweet. The tourist association warns that tea reception may pause during particularly busy periods. Check current prices and availability before buying.

faq.question: Do these places keep the same opening arrangements at New Year?
faq.answer: Do not assume so. Hokokuji lists closure from December 29 to January 3, while the other sites may have ceremonies and special arrangements. This is an evergreen first-visit selection rather than a holiday programme; check each place’s notices for your exact dates.

conclusion: A first visit to Kamakura works best when the places that interest you match a clear travel plan. Start with the Hase pair and central shrine; add Hokokuji’s bamboo or Zeniarai’s tradition when you have enough time. Check final admissions, respect the sites’ religious use and leave room between visits. Five places then become a way to choose your own route, rather than a list to finish at any pace.
